statement: Another technical challenge is that we do not know the almost 6-uniform hypergraph GM as we only have access to the 3-uniform hypergraph G and predictor P which may provide incorrect guesses. To deal with it, we use the approach outlined above (and fully described in Algorithm 1) instantiated with the matching predictor P ; specifically, we remove the guesses after a predetermined number of recovery steps. We now formalize our setting by defining the necessary predictor that takes a single element as input and outputs at most λ elements. U  ▶ Definition 1. Given a class C of sets, we call a predictor P : U → ≤λ a matching predictor for C if for any A ∈ C, there is a matching M containing an (1 − o(1))-fraction of elements of A such that for any edge {x, y} of M , we have that y ∈ P (x) and x ∈ P (y). Furthermore, for any x ∈ U, P (x) can be computed in polynomial time with respect to |P (x)|.

However, we do not quite obtain a 6-uniform hypergraph as the matching M may leave a sublinear number of elements unmatched and moreover, by merging the hyperedges of x and y for {x, y} ∈ M , we may obtain a hyperedge with less than six vertices as the hyperedges of x and y may share one or more vertices. Another technical challenge is that we do not know the almost 6-uniform hypergraph GM as we only have access to the 3-uniform hypergraph G and predictor P which may provide incorrect guesses. To deal with it, we use the approach outlined above (and fully described in Algorithm 1) instantiated with the matching predictor P ; specifically, we remove the guesses after a predetermined number of recovery steps. We now formalize our setting by defining the necessary predictor that takes a single element as input and outputs at most λ elements. U  ▶ Definition 1. Furthermore, for any x ∈ U, P (x) can be computed in polynomial time with respect to |P (x)|.
